stem: A client with Graves' disease develops bulging eyes and swelling of the tissues around the eyes. How should the nurse interpret these findings?

options.A: They are characteristic of Graves' ophthalmopathy, also called thyroid eye disease
options.B: They indicate diabetic retinopathy caused by chronic hyperglycemia
options.C: They indicate acute angle-closure glaucoma caused by impaired aqueous drainage
options.D: They are expected effects of every cause of hyperthyroidism

rationale: The American Thyroid Association describes Graves' ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease) as inflammation and swelling of tissues around the eyes that may cause eye bulging in people with Graves' disease. Therefore A is the best answer. Diabetic retinopathy and acute angle-closure glaucoma are different ocular disorders, and the ATA specifically notes that Graves' disease is the form of hyperthyroidism associated with this inflammatory eye syndrome rather than the finding being expected with every cause of hyperthyroidism.
educational_objective: Recognize bulging eyes with orbital tissue swelling in a client with Graves' disease as Graves' ophthalmopathy/thyroid eye disease.
source_locator: Section 'Eye disease': Graves' disease can be associated with eye inflammation, swelling of tissues around the eyes, and bulging of the eyes (Graves' ophthalmopathy/orbitopathy)
source_claim_supported: Graves' disease may cause Graves' ophthalmopathy/thyroid eye disease with inflammation, tissue swelling around the eyes, and bulging eyes.

correction_summary: Removed the family-member narrative and the overbroad wording that the eye finding is simply a 'distinctive feature specifically' without naming the clinical syndrome. Reframed the item to identify Graves' ophthalmopathy/thyroid eye disease, used the current ATA Graves' disease page with an exact locator, and rebuilt distractors as genuine alternative ocular interpretations plus the overgeneralization to all hyperthyroidism. Difficulty adjusted from hard to easy.
audit_findings: A is directly supported by ATA. B and C are separate eye disorders without the Graves-specific orbital inflammatory context; D conflicts with ATA's distinction that this eye syndrome is associated with Graves' disease rather than expected across all causes of hyperthyroidism. The diagnosis is anchored by known Graves' disease plus the source-defined eye findings, so no second answer or hidden assumption remains.
